prompt.context: Our client is a national convenience store chain that has historically been the market leader in frozen slushy drinks. Recently, other brands are entering the frozen slushy drink market, and the client has hired our team to create a strategy to build brand equity.
prompt.question: What ideas can you come up with to build our client's frozen slushy drink brand?

clarifying_info.q: Where are the drinks currently sold?
clarifying_info.a: Currently, the drinks are sold only on premise in the convenience stores.
The target market is generally children.

clarifying_info.q: Is this similar to a Slurpee?
What is the scope of ideas we should consider?
clarifying_info.a: Any ideas are on the table — anything to build brand equity and awareness to maintain the drink's #1 market position (in terms of revenue dollars, not profit or unit volume).

framework: Identify current brand equity drivers (in-store visibility, brand recognition, loyalty)
Explore distribution expansion — new channels beyond convenience stores
Evaluate partnership opportunities — venues frequented by target audience (children/families)
Assess marketing and promotional levers (advertising, packaging, events)
Consider product extension or innovation to differentiate from new entrants
Evaluate each idea on: branding impact, target audience fit, cost, and margin/price point

questions.prompt: Question 1: What ideas do you have for building brand equity for the frozen slushy drinks?
questions.guidance: Candidate should produce a structured, creative list organized by category. Interviewer should push with 'What else?' to expand. Key ideas to probe for if not raised: selling at amusement parks and selling at a popular fast food chain (e.g., McDonald's). Creativity and structure are equally important here.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Let's think more closely about two ideas — selling at amusement parks and at fast food restaurants. What factors would you use to evaluate each idea?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare the two channels across multiple dimensions. Strong answers cover: (1) Branding impact — amusement park is positive (no on-site competition, captive audience); fast food is negative (brand competes with/is overshadowed by the fast food brand). (2) Target audience fit — both are positive since kids and families frequent both. (3) Cost — amusement park is neutral (expensive infrastructure build-out); fast food is positive (infrastructure already in place). (4) Margin/price point — amusement park is positive (can charge premium prices); fast food is negative (low price expectations). Any additional factors should be evaluated appropriately.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Given the list we just created, what idea would you pursue and why? Also, what costs do we need to consider in undertaking this project at an amusement park?
questions.guidance: Either channel can be justified, but the amusement park is marginally better: ability to charge higher prices without diluting the brand or competing with another food brand's offerings. For costs, candidate should distinguish fixed from variable. Fixed: initial build-out of space (plumbing, counters, machinery, signage); operating overhead; labor. Variable: cups, straws, lids, ingredients.

questions.prompt: Question 4: What percentage of amusement park guests need to buy a slushy drink to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should treat the initial build-out as a sunk cost and focus on annual fixed costs vs. contribution margin. Arriving at ~2.6% and recognizing this is a low, achievable hurdle is the key insight.

math.setup: Annual fixed costs: operating overhead $100,000 + labor $100,000 = $200,000. Variable cost per unit: cups $0.20 + straws $0.15 + lids $0.15 + ingredients $0.50 = $1.00. Price per drink: $7.00. Contribution margin: $7.00 - $1.00 = $6.00. Average annual attendees: 1,300,000.
math.answer: Approximately 2.6% of annual amusement park attendees need to purchase a slushy to break even. This is a very low hurdle, supporting the viability of the idea.

questions.guidance: Candidate should tie the recommendation back to the original brief (build brand equity, defend #1 market position). A strong recommendation covers: (1) pursue amusement park expansion to build brand equity; (2) financially viable — less than 3% of attendees need to buy to break even; (3) high-margin operation; (4) low upfront build-out cost relative to revenue potential; (5) ideal brand-building venue — captive family/child audience with no direct on-site competition.

brainstorming.prompt: What ideas do you have for building brand equity for the frozen slushy drinks?

categories.name: New Distribution Channels
ideas: Sell at amusement parks (captive audience, premium pricing)
Partner with fast food chains (e.g., McDonald's) for co-branded drinks
Expand to movie theaters
Sell at sports stadiums and arenas
Expand to grocery/big-box retail in branded take-home format

categories.name: Partnerships and Co-Branding
ideas: Co-brand with popular children's movie/TV franchises
Partner with sports leagues or teams targeting youth
Collaborate with schools or youth events

categories.name: Marketing and Promotions
ideas: Launch a loyalty/rewards program
Run limited-edition seasonal flavors to drive excitement
Increase in-store merchandising and signage
Social media campaigns targeting kids and parents
Sponsor youth-oriented events and community activities

categories.name: Product Innovation
ideas: Introduce new flavors or flavor combinations
Create collectible branded cups
Offer customizable mix-your-own options
Develop a lower-sugar or healthier variant to expand audience

categories.name: Digital and Experiential
ideas: Build a brand mascot and associated content/media
Create branded games or apps tied to the drink
Pop-up events at festivals and fairs

recommendation: Pursue expansion into amusement parks as the primary brand equity building strategy
The amusement park channel targets the core audience (children and families), allows premium pricing ($7/drink), and requires less than 3% of annual attendees to purchase to break even
risks: High upfront infrastructure cost ($100,000 build-out) requires capital commitment per location
Revenue is seasonal — amusement park attendance is concentrated in summer months
Negotiations with amusement park operators may require revenue sharing, compressing margins
next_steps: Identify target amusement parks and initiate partnership discussions
Develop a detailed P&L model incorporating seasonality and revenue share
Design the on-site build-out specification and procurement plan
Pilot at one or two parks before national rollout
Track brand awareness metrics pre- and post-launch to validate equity impact
